full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Professor David Mba, Vice-Chancellor of Birmingham City University.

What does it tell us about the skills system when we can have newly qualified nurses struggling to find nursing jobs at the same time as we worry about the NHS’s workforce capacity?

That was the striking backdrop to the Government’s ‘Graduate Guarantee’ for newly qualified nurses and midwives in England last summer. NHS England said every newly qualified nurse and midwife would have the opportunity to apply to join the health and social care workforce, with providers encouraged to recruit ahead of vacancies and make greater use of newly qualified staff. It also asked NHS organisations to work with local universities and system partners to improve access to roles across health and care.

It was a welcome response to a very practical problem. But it also exposes something much bigger about the way we talk about skills in England.

We tend to talk about skills as though the difficulty is producing qualified people. The nursing experience exposes that qualification is only one part of the story. There is a difference between educating someone, qualifying them, employing them, deploying them where they are needed and retaining them in the workforce. That distinction matters well beyond nursing.

The problem is not simply producing graduates

A nursing workforce problem can quickly become a conversation about graduates. And a conversation about graduates can quickly become a conversation about universities. Before long, the debate risks becoming about the number, type and status of degrees, rather than the much bigger question of what kind of education and training system we need to meet the country’s skills needs.

The nursing guarantee is revealing precisely because it is not simply about producing more nurses. The challenge is connecting newly qualified professionals with jobs, employers and places where their skills are needed. That brings recruitment cycles, vacancy distribution, geography, job design and workforce planning into the picture, alongside universities.

In other words, the skills challenge sits across a system.

That should change the way we think about excellence in higher education, and it matters because excellence in English higher education is not judged in a vacuum. A powerful hierarchy of institutional prestige shapes which forms of education and contribution are most visible and valued.

England has built a higher education system in which one particular institutional model carries enormous cultural and political weight. Research intensity has become an unusually powerful proxy for institutional excellence. Research funding, rankings, prestige and media attention all contribute to a hierarchy in which research-intensive universities are often treated as the benchmark against which other forms of higher education are judged.

There is nothing wrong with research excellence. England needs globally competitive research universities, and their contribution to innovation, productivity and scientific discovery is substantial. The problem is what happens when the strengths of that model become the organising principle for the wider skills system.

Excellence is not the same as workforce development

The skills England needs are not all research skills. They include nurses, teachers, engineers, technicians, digital professionals, construction workers, social care professionals and people able to apply new technologies in workplaces. Meeting those needs requires professional education, work-integrated learning, employer partnerships, apprenticeships, flexible provision and opportunities for adults to retrain and upskill.

Practice-based education is not simply academic education with more workplace experience. It brings disciplinary knowledge together with professional practice, real-world problem solving and the needs of employers and public services. In many fields, the ability to apply knowledge effectively in complex professional settings is itself a form of educational excellence.

Many of the institutions that are particularly strong at this work are not research-intensive universities. They educate large numbers of mature, commuter, part-time and first-generation students, and supply the workforce of the places in which they are based. Their contribution to innovation may be less visible than a patent or a research citation, but it can be just as consequential: improving public services, changing professional practice, helping SMEs adopt new technology and developing the skills of local workforces.

Nursing makes the point particularly clearly. We can train and qualify someone, but that is only one part of building a workforce. The system also needs to connect a graduate with an employer, a role and a place where their skills are needed – and then create the conditions in which they can build a career and stay.

That is not an argument against research universities. It is an argument for recognising that workforce development is itself a form of excellence.

A problem of prestige?

For decades, the strongest educational signal available to ambitious young people has been the traditional academic higher education route. Russell Group membership has become shorthand for educational quality in ways that extend well beyond research.

That signal matters because prestige affects behaviour. It affects what schools celebrate, what parents aspire to, what students think they should apply for, and what policymakers see as a successful higher education system. It can also affect which forms of learning are perceived as being for the ‘best’ students.

This creates a paradox.

We can say, quite reasonably, that England needs more technical, professional, applied and vocational skills, while simultaneously maintaining a system in which some of the routes most closely associated with those capabilities have lower status. But perhaps the prestige trap is not that research excellence is valued too highly. It is that one particular form of excellence can become the template against which every other contribution is judged.

What if the measures we use to identify higher education excellence are simply better at seeing some forms of contribution than others?

A higher education institution can make an extraordinary contribution to nursing through research, clinical innovation and advanced professional education. Another can contribute through educating large numbers of nurses, working with NHS employers, supporting placements and helping graduates build careers in the region.

Both contributions matter. They are simply different. The answer is not to diminish academic education. It is to stop treating academic education as the only credible definition of educational ambition.

Skills require a more diverse system

This is where institutional diversity matters.

Teaching-intensive universities often have a different relationship with their local economies and public services. They educate large numbers of mature, commuter and part-time students, work closely with employers and professional partners, and provide routes into the occupations that communities depend upon.

At Birmingham City University, our graduates make a significant contribution to the city’s workforce and public services, with 40 per cent of our first-degree graduates staying in Birmingham to start their careers. In the West Midlands, BCU trains 43 per cent of new nurses. This is an example of what an anchor institution can mean to a regional skills ecosystem: educating the professionals who sustain the public services and wider economy of the place it serves.

This is not a plea to divide universities into research and teaching institutions, still less to suggest that one is inherently better than the other.

Russell Group universities increasingly provide professional education, engage with employers and develop apprenticeships. Nor should we romanticise the alternatives: teaching-intensive institutions face their own challenges, and not every applied or vocational course automatically delivers better outcomes for students or employers.

But institutional diversity should mean more than allowing different universities to exist alongside one another. It should mean recognising that different institutions can make different contributions to national objectives.

In short, we require a broader definition of excellence.

Not too much higher education, but too narrow a conception of what it is for

We tell young people that the most academically selective universities represent the pinnacle of educational success; we measure institutional success through metrics that privilege research; and then we wonder why technical, professional and vocational pathways struggle to command equivalent status.

The answer is not to diminish the Russell Group. It is to stop asking it, implicitly or otherwise, to provide the template for the whole system.

The nursing guarantee offers a useful way into this debate because it exposes the limits of thinking about skills as qualifications alone. If the question is ‘how many graduates do we need?’, we will naturally look first to universities and qualifications. If the question is ‘what capabilities does the economy and society need, where are they needed, and what is the best way to develop, deploy and retain them?’, the answer becomes much more complicated. It also changes how we should think about the contribution of universities.

A higher education institution’s contribution to the economy might be a scientific breakthrough. It might also be a nurse who stays in the region, an adult learner who retrains mid-career, a new approach to professional practice, or a partnership that helps a small business, charity or community organisation develop its workforce. All are forms of capability. Not all are equally visible in the measures by which institutional prestige is constructed.

England needs world-leading research universities. It also needs universities and colleges that excel at professional education, applied learning, regional workforce development and lifelong skills. These are not competing ambitions. The challenge for policymakers is to create a system in which these different forms of excellence reinforce rather than compete with one another.

The nursing guarantee reminds us that having the right qualification is not the same as having the right skills system. Perhaps we need to apply the same lesson to higher education.

If England is serious about productivity, regional growth, public service reform and lifelong learning, we need a definition of excellence broad enough to recognise not only the knowledge universities create, but the capabilities they build – and the people, places and communities those capabilities ultimately serve.

title: 2027 College Free Speech Rankings: Kirk murder adds another difficult topic to dismal climate for student expression
summary: The assassination of Charlie Kirk generated a wave of censorship at America's colleges over the past year, further contributing to a climate in which too many students do not feel free to express themselves on campus.
full_text:
The University of Chicago takes the top spot, while Texas State University, the University of Washington, and New York University sit at the bottom

Most difficult topics for students to discuss on campus include the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, Donald Trump, Charlie Kirk, and abortion

Some schools fall in rankings following Charlie Kirk-related controversies

121 of the 261 schools ranked got an “F” for their speech climate

WASHINGTON, Sept. 9, 2026 – The assassination of Charlie Kirk generated a wave of censorship at America's colleges over the past year, further contributing to a climate in which too many students fear expressing themselves on campus.

Encouragingly, the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression’s seventh annual College Free Speech Rankings found the percentage of students who said it was acceptable to shout down a speaker, block entry to a campus speech, or use violence to stop a campus speech declined slightly from last year’s record highs.

The survey’s average overall score (61.36) is the highest recorded in seven years but still corresponds to a D- on the report’s grading scale, an unacceptable state of affairs.

“At a tumultuous time for higher education, we are seeing some progress in campus free speech policies and indications that students may be less willing to tolerate shoutdowns and violence on campus compared to recent years,” said FIRE President and CEO Greg Lukianoff. “But the overall state of free speech on campus is grim. Too many college administrators wield their power to cancel controversial speakers, cave to government or student calls for censorship, and limit academic freedom. This report emphasizes the need for colleges to embrace their constitutional obligations wholeheartedly.”

The rankings of 261 schools encompass almost 63,000 student responses to a wide array of free speech-related questions. Looming over this year’s report was the September 10, 2025, murder of conservative activist Charlie Kirk at Utah Valley University. At 61 of the ranked schools, over half of students say Kirk is “difficult to discuss” on campus, and nine schools that punished faculty over Kirk-related comments lost points in the rankings. Additionally, some campus chapters of Kirk’s group Turning Point USA have been denied recognition or faced calls for their derecognition as an official student organization.

“The impact of Charlie Kirk’s assassination continues to negatively reverberate on campuses across the country,” said FIRE Chief Researcher Sean Stevens. “Rather than view the tragedy as a warning about the extreme results of partisanship and inability to peacefully engage in dialogue, many college admins took it as an invitation to double down on censorship.”

The highest-ranked colleges for free speech:

1. University of Chicago

2. Claremont McKenna College

3. Georgia Institute of Technology-Main Campus

4. Michigan Technological University

5. Vanderbilt University

6. Dartmouth College

7. Purdue University-Main Campus

8. Appalachian State University

9. University of Virginia-Main Campus

10. George Mason University

The lowest-ranked colleges for free speech:

252. Howard University

253. University of Miami

254. Loyola University Chicago

255. Boston College

256. Indiana University-Bloomington

257. Rutgers University-New Brunswick

258. Northeastern University

259. Texas State University

260. University of Washington-Seattle Campus

261. New York University

EXPLORE THE RANKINGS

Speech controversies at the highest-rated schools are rare, and students say their administrations are more likely to support free speech. For the third time, the University of Chicago has claimed the top spot in the rankings, and the schools that improved their score the most include Harvard University and the University of California, Davis. After coming in dead last in the 2024 and 2025 rankings, Harvard’s ranking rose by only a few places last year. But this year, its ranking rose dramatically after students reported that, compared to last year, they felt their administration more strongly protects freedom of speech and that they are more comfortable expressing controversial political views on campus.

One hundred and twenty-one of the 261 schools ranked got an F for their speech climate, while only 24 schools received a speech climate grade of C or higher. The lowest-rated schools have restrictive speech policies and some of last year’s most shocking anti-free speech moments. Several incidents cited in the report include:

The terminations of Thomas Alter, a tenured professor of history, and Idris Robinson, a professor of philosophy by Texas State University, for off-campus protected expression.

Multiple disruptions, attempted disruptions, and event cancellations — six in total since 2024 — at the University of Washington.

The cancellation of a planned lecture by Raz Segal, an Israeli historian and genocide scholar, after the Northeastern University Police Department demanded a list of names of all the registered attendees.

Students at New York University were barred by administrators from inviting multiple performers affiliated with No Music For Genocide to the university’s annual V100 concert, which is organized and planned by students and student organizations.

“Even for those schools perpetually at the bottom of the rankings, it’s never too late to right the ship,” said FIRE Vice President of Research Angela C. Erickson. “Only 40% of students said that it was ‘extremely’ or ‘very’ clear that their administration protects free speech on campus. College administrators need the humility to reform policies and systems that leave students afraid to speak their minds, and the courage to shut down deplatformings and disruptions when others try to silence them. A great education requires both: the freedom to speak and the opportunity to hear ideas you might otherwise never encounter.”

Explore the full rankings here.

The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit organization dedicated to defending and sustaining the individual rights of all Americans to free speech and free thought—the most essential qualities of liberty. FIRE recognizes that colleges and universities play a vital role in preserving free thought within a free society. To this end, we place a special emphasis on defending the individual rights of students and faculty members on our nation’s campuses, including freedom of speech, freedom of association, due process, legal equality, religious liberty, and sanctity of conscience.

title: USC earns FIRE's top rating for free speech
summary: With the new “green light” rating, the University of Southern California’s retabulated ranking would be 37th nationally in FIRE’s College Free Speech Rankings, 179 places higher than its ranking a year ago.
full_text:
LOS ANGELES, Sept. 9, 2026 — The University of Southern California has earned a “green light” rating from the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, the organization’s highest rating for university policies governing expression.

FIRE awards the rating to institutions whose written policies pose no serious threat to student speech. Of the 493 colleges and universities rated by FIRE, only 77 earn a green light rating, or around 16%. And of the 45 California colleges and universities rated by FIRE, only three in addition to USC earn a green light rating.

“There are hundreds of universities with eloquent commitments to free inquiry and policies that quietly undercut them. On its own initiative, USC worked with us to close that gap. It has earned the green light rating.” — Laura Beltz, FIRE Director of Policy Reform

Since becoming USC’s president last year, Beong-Soo Kim has made open dialogue a foundational priority of his administration. Part of that commitment has involved working to ensure the university’s policies fully support and encourage a culture of robust dialogue and debate. Under President Kim’s leadership, USC made changes to its policies governing events, posting, and conduct that does not rise to the level of prohibited harassment. FIRE has also determined that USC’s policies around institutional neutrality now substantially mirror the Chicago Statement, the model policy adopted by roughly 120 university administrations and faculty bodies nationwide.

“Open dialogue is easy to support in principle but more difficult to ingrain in the culture and actions of a university. USC is 100% committed to that work, which is foundational to everything we do – educating future leaders, advancing cutting-edge research, and upholding the principles of freedom and democracy.” — Beong-Soo Kim, President, University of Southern California

USC’s new rating also means that it will receive a substantial boost in FIRE’s annual College Free Speech Rankings going forward. Because USC’s green light rating took effect after FIRE’s June 1 data collection deadline, the 2027 rankings released on September 9 reflect USC’s prior policies. USC’s retabulated score would have placed 37th in FIRE’s 2027 College Free Speech Rankings, 179 places higher than its ranking a year ago and among the top 15% of schools ranked.

USC’s green light rating reflects other initiatives undertaken by the university under President Kim’s leadership, including the launch of the USC Open Dialogue Project, a university-wide effort encouraging students, faculty, and staff to engage seriously across differences in perspective and opinion. In its first nine months, the program convened 25 events with 24 campus and external partners, drawing more than 2,000 attendees. Programming ranged from debates over hate speech and standardized testing to conversations with public figures representing a broad range of perspectives.

Institutions interested in earning a green light rating can contact FIRE’s Policy Reform team at speechcodes@fire.org.

About FIRE

The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit organization dedicated to defending and sustaining the individual rights of all Americans to free speech and free thought—the most essential qualities of liberty. FIRE recognizes that colleges and universities play a vital role in preserving free thought within a free society. To this end, we place a special emphasis on defending the individual rights of students and faculty members on our nation’s campuses, including freedom of speech, freedom of association, due process, legal equality, religious liberty, and sanctity of conscience.

About USC

Founded in 1880, the University of Southern California is one of the world’s leading academic research institutions with 23 schools, a multi-billion-dollar health enterprise and a vast research and development engine. The university enrolls 46,000 highly accomplished undergraduate and graduate students and employs 4,600 faculty who are members of major national academies, and MacArthur, Academy Award and Pulitzer Prize winners, among many others. USC has a nationally recognized athletic program and a passionate global network of 500,000 alumni — the Trojan Family. Located in the heart of Los Angeles, USC is a powerhouse of innovation and impact with a global reach.

full_text:
Private colleges are offering discounts to rush students into a diploma the federal government is cancelling over concerns it is being “misused by shonks”.

The government announced in early September it would deregister the graduate diploma of management (learning) which it suspected was being used by “non-genuine” students to remain in Australia. The course is taught by close to 450 institutions, has over 15,000 students studying currently and more than 40,000 students registered for future enrolment following completion of a different vocational course.

Ads posted to social media and shared among agents and students in recent days encouraged students to join the course or expedite their start date before cancellation on 5 October. Any students already enrolled and studying by that date are allowed to complete it.

Some immigration education agents have offered promotions for the month of September, including in WhatsApp messages and texts, encouraging students to join the course or those who have a future enrolment to study now. Several ads promote discounted course fees or a free certificate of enrolment to join immediately.

One private college has sent immigration agents a promotion offering “attractive” commissions with same-day offer letters and confirmation of enrolment for students, with two “special intakes” on 21 September and 2 October – just three days before the course is cancelled.

Phil Honeywood, the chief executive of the International Education Association of Australia (IEAA), supported the decision to cancel the course and said it could put some private providers trying to loophole the system into financial trouble.

“The government for all the right reasons moved to stop non-genuine international students from using this course to stay in the country,” Honeywood said.

“High-quality providers will always have a place in the international education ecosystem … they would rather have these factory-type private providers out of the system for all the right reasons.”

Some education migration providers are encouraging the more than 40,000 international students with a future enrolment to start the course now before it is cancelled. Some of those students would need to do so, or choose a different course such as a bachelor’s or master’s with a high qualification level to maintain their visa conditions. That could mean completing two courses at the same time.

Students who have “packaged” a lower-level vocational course with the graduate diploma to be completed after, will need to enrol into a higher-level course to maintain their visa requirements.

One student who spoke to Guardian Australia on the condition of anonymity said they had initially come to Australia to study a bachelor’s degree but unenrolled after one semester on the advice of a migration agent to do a VET course in carpentry, followed by the graduate diploma in management. The graduate diploma and the VET course would fulfil the qualification level required to maintain a valid international student visa.

They said they were being told to commence the graduate diploma now.

“I talked to the agent, and they told me the new rules. They want me to study concurrently, [so] I can study both courses at the same time. I don’t know if I can take this much study load,” the international student said.

They said other friends doing the same course pathway were also given the same advice, and were also stressed by the potential workload.

A migration agent, who asked not to be named, said they had heard of other agents and institutions pushing students to expedite their enrolment, but they warned the government would view this suspiciously. They said they were concerned that this behaviour would damage the reputation and credibility of the rest of the sector.

They also said private institutions might look at setting up other courses such as the graduate diploma of strategic leadership that just over 34 colleges currently teach or the graduate diploma of portfolio management that is taught by just a few, that have the same visa requirement level.

Julian Hill, the assistant minister responsible for cancelling the course, said the department and education regulator would be “closely watching student and provider behaviour”.

“Students and providers are on notice that curious patterns of early commencement or new enrolments will be investigated and action taken against those doing the wrong thing,” Hill told Guardian Australia.

At the time of the announcement in September that the course would be deregistered, Hill said in a statement: “The Coalition left behind a shocking mess in 2022, with unsustainably high growth in student numbers in the least reputable parts of the sector, and our high-quality student visa being degraded into a low-rent illegal work visa and misused by shonks.”

Melanie McFarlane, New South Wales president of the Migration Institute of Australia, said some education agents were helping their students into master’s courses to maintain their visas.

“Those students needing to find an alternate course, they’re being placed by, I would say, reputable agents, into a master’s degree within the same institution where that graduate diploma was otherwise available,” she said.

“But then you’ve got the other side where there are migration agents who are potentially going out of business because of all the changes to the industry … and might be rushing students into that course in the time that they can.”

It is part of a wider crackdown by the government to curb visa-hopping and overstayers in Australia.

The government has now banned international students from starting one qualification and then transferring to a lower-value qualification which would allow them to remain in the country and work more hours instead of studying. This would help prevent a student enrolled in a bachelor’s degree from downgrading to a vocational course.

Hill said the government had also banned commissions for agents transferring students between courses in Australia.

“This has helped but the quantum and pattern of transfers remains concerning, so from next year international students looking to change providers will have to apply for [a] new visa.”

title: ‘I’d like to explain why I was such a monster back then’: six writers on the apologies they wish they’d made
summary:
From making life hell for a young teacher to doubting the motives of a caring foster mother, Olivia Petter, Derek Owusu, Annie Lord and other writers repent for past bad behaviour

full_text:
Olivia Petter: ‘We hid in cupboards behind Ms Hill’s desk and jumped out to frighten her halfway through lessons’

At school, I was not a good girl. Actually, that’s putting it mildly: I was an emotional terrorist hellbent on inflicting torture and humiliation on my year 6 teacher, Ms Hill, one whoopee cushion at a time. That’s how it began, anyway, but like all crimes, mine followed a strategic pattern of escalation, carefully executed alongside my best friend and accomplice.

We started small: bringing spiders into Ms Hill’s classroom; writing silly notes on the whiteboard; replacing her precious chocolate digestives with stale biscuits from the dining hall. Then we took things further, hiding in cupboards behind her desk and jumping out to frighten her halfway through lessons, and, on one occasion, exploiting the bathroom’s faulty taps to flood the entire thing over lunchtime.

None of this was OK. In fact, it was downright awful, a symptom of reckless malevolence fuelled by boredom and entitlement. We were just unhappy kids who wanted to watch the world burn – an operation that poor Ms Hill bore almost all of the brunt of. To be clear, we never did anything that would constitute harassment, but our pranks were consistent and cruel.

Looking back on them as an adult with several friends who work as teachers, I can’t help but feel a deep sense of shame and guilt. I owe Ms Hill a proper apology. And, while I won’t attempt to justify my 11-year-old self’s behaviour, I’d like to offer an explanation as to why I might have been such a little monster back then.

Like so many other kids, I was being bullied, as was my best friend. I can remember one breaktime when she was pushed up against a wall by one of the older girls, who threatened to physically hurt her. Then there were the other classic things girls do to one another: leaving people out, spreading malicious rumours, and generally finding new and innovative ways to put people down to make others laugh. Neither one of us felt as if we fitted in, and so we stuck together.

There were issues going on at home – my parents divorced and my dad was living between London and the US. And I wasn’t really sleeping, either; I had bouts of insomnia as a child. In other words, I was struggling, and doing poorly at school as a result. A newly qualified twentysomething teacher in charge of our class, Ms Hill was the one often reprimanding us for not getting the grades we should have been – it was a highly competitive school, so I suspect she was under pressure to make sure her pupils were meeting certain standards. Again, as kids, we didn’t know that. All we saw was a young teacher telling us we weren’t good enough, and being mean to us in the process. So we decided to be mean back.

I really regret the way my friend and I behaved back then. Because, even though on the surface this might have looked like innocuous mischief, I can imagine it took a toll. Nobody deserves to be humiliated in their place of work, especially not by obnoxious children with far too much time on their hands. So, Ms Hill, if you’re still around, please accept my apology. I’m sorry for all the whoopee cushions, for stealing your biscuits, and for attempting to embarrass you to mask my own feelings of inadequacy. Ultimately, I hope my behaviour made you laugh more times than it made you frown. And that you are living a happy, fulfilled life somewhere with unlimited supplies of McVitie’s and absolutely no spiders.

Olivia Petter is a journalist and author of Gold Rush.

Derek Owusu: ‘Why did you foster us – why not other children, lighter in tone and burden, closer to those you had brought up?’

Mum, why don’t I remember more about you? So much is missing. I had 10 years with you: seven before I was returned to my biological mother, and three broken up into Christmas visits, with photos I have since lost and sweets sometimes arriving in the post. I tell myself you died when I was 10, but maybe it was later. Maybe you were kept from me to help me move on, just like your death was kept from me until I turned 14.

The last Christmas visit I remember well enough: the huge stocking with socks and satsumas at the bottom, imitation Game Boys, all surrounded by chocolate gold coins that sometimes cut you before they revealed the goods. Then, 10 of us around the kitchen table, crackers pulled and hats donned, jokes read to straight faces or a quick “oi” and glance down the table from you, and then, finally, the wait. Everyone had to be finished before we could run to the tree, and whoever was last received Christmas knocks on their head when you weren’t looking.

These are the images I come back to. So many children running around your house, so much noise, so much joy and, of course, so much lost. Because each child was away from their parent(s), long‑term or short-term, but each child called you Mum, regardless of duration, regardless of difference.

And we were different. All black children living with a very white mother, from dressing us up for Remembrance Day – flat cap and shoe polish – to awkwardly cutting our afros with scissors and never worrying about moistening our scalps. So I ask why. Why did you foster us – why not other children, lighter in tone and burden, closer to those you had brought up? You had seven children of your own, I think, and grandchildren who surely could have allowed you to relive those years.

I never got to ask, so I grew up speculating. Were you a white saviour, I asked myself. Was it Christian virtue? Was there more going on, more that I can’t remember, or choose not to?

It could have simply been about the money. You had retired, and perhaps you needed the income, though I remember your husband working. Perhaps it was greed, the four-bedroom house with a garage and garden not enough. I asked myself all this and more, fictionalised you and then questioned you, tried to uncover something suppressed.

Until, with time, with differing perspectives, I turned the why on myself. Why must there be something more? The money – the fee charged for private foster care that my biological mum paid monthly – you took a quarter of it and put it into a secret account, which became mine when I turned 16. Our race wasn’t your choice; it was more that private foster care was the safest alternative for west African immigrants, ones anxious about sending their children back to where they started, even if they struggled to find footing on the troubled ground of Britain.

You were no saviour, because you were imperfect and made no attempt to hide it. You taught us lessons but presented them harshly, maybe too harshly, the cane by the window sill evidence of your impatience. But you apologised when you were wrong, acknowledged when we had done right. And kept going even when sick, when dying, trying to fight for the last of us.

There is a story I remember, of one of the foster kids almost being deported with his family. And the person they immediately called was you. You drove to the airport, in that beat-up van we loved to pile into, picked up the child, and said you’d keep them safe for as long as was necessary.

I need to let kindness be. I wish I had let you be, returning your compassion with some form of empathy. So, Mum, I am sorry. I’m sorry I failed to see you and I am sorry for my doubt.

Derek Owusu is a writer and poet. His third novel, The Recovery House, is out now.

It’s a fresh spring afternoon, but inside the hermetically sealed corridor of the students’ union, the air is thick with body heat and desperation. Through clouds of Lynx Africa and BO comes an incessant thrum: whispered soliloquies, hummed arpeggios, the rustle of photocopied scripts. Next to me, a boy repeats his own name over and over as though, faced with the impatient stare of a third-year student cosplaying as a theatre director, he might forget this most elementary fact about himself. When my turn comes, I summon the confidence I’ve been trying to assemble over the previous six months.

The theatre society was full of extraordinary talent, but all of the best performances happened off the stage. University offered all of us the same irresistible bargain: here, finally, we could become whoever we wanted to be. New friends. New politics. New haircuts. We dressed like people we had seen in films, smoked because interesting people smoked, half-read Judith Butler, and spoke with the unique certainty of bright 19-year-olds.

That was the backdrop to our meeting. You were the rosy-cheeked girl in the director’s chair and I was your leading man. And from there we both played our parts perfectly until everything fell apart. Three months together at university felt like three years anywhere else. We rehearsed together, got blind drunk together, and learned each other’s childhood stories with the urgency of people convinced life was already slipping away.

I’m sorry that when we met I couldn’t really see you. You were funny and warm and emotionally fluent in a way I wouldn’t be for years. You were trying, with remarkable generosity, to know me. The trouble was that I was entirely invested in remaining unknowable.

I already knew I was gay. Or rather, I knew in the way people know the things they cannot yet afford to admit. It was my Big Secret: a stolen penny burning a hole in my pocket.

I walked into that audition room full of false and careful bravado, and saw what I thought might be my salvation in your smile. I don’t think I dated you because I wanted to deceive you. I fell for you because I wanted to deceive myself. I imagine the distinction matters far less when you’re the one who gets hurt.

If there was ever a moment, afterwards, when you wondered whether there had been something lacking in you, then I am deeply sorry. There wasn’t. The thing that wasn’t whole was me, and I mistook that incompleteness for a problem that could be solved by somebody else filling in the gaps.

Growing up has involved many apologies. Some I’ve made. Some I’ve only rehearsed. This one sticks in my throat because it asks me to admit something I still find uncomfortable: that becoming yourself is not, by itself, a virtue. It matters how you do it, who gets caught in the machinery. I was so intent on becoming someone I could live with that I forgot you were living through it, too.

People often say university is where you find yourself. That wasn’t quite true for me. University was where I finally stopped pretending it was possible to be somebody else. The irony, of course, is that I had joined the one society statistically least likely to cure me of being gay. Somewhere between Annie Get Your Gun, the Sondheim medley and the cancelled production of Rent, the evidence was mounting.

Auditions are strange things. You spend two minutes pretending to be somebody else in the hope that someone will finally see who you are. I spent much longer pretending. I’m sorry you had to watch.

William Rayfet Hunter is a writer and author of Sunstruck.

Poorna Bell: ‘I went into a diatribe about how that woman was such a phoney. “I’m standing right behind you,” a voice said’

As nicknames go, Foghorn Leghorn – inspired by the oversized cartoon rooster with a booming voice – isn’t particularly agreeable to me, but it has been fairly accurate. When combined with alcohol, this tendency can create a toxic cocktail, and leads to me saying obnoxious things at a high volume, often about someone as they stand undetected, mere feet away.

I haven’t drunk alcohol for 16 months, primarily because it was making my body feel like a garbage pail, and with newfound sobriety comes a reckoning about some of the things I did and said while under the influence. It’s not exactly a 12-step list of amends, but it’s close.

About 11 years ago, I was going to a press awards ceremony held at the Grosvenor hotel in London. I didn’t particularly want to go as it required a late night and an early start the next day, and it was this bedrock of grumbling that was my undoing. Sometimes I can be a cheerful drunk, but other times it taps into some unexpressed reservoir of resentment, and it was this that flowed into my bloodstream along with a lot of white wine.

Early in the evening, a woman in her 20s came up to say hello. We didn’t know each other well, but I remembered her from an internal work event a couple of months prior. We made small talk at the bar, which then turned slightly awkward as we ran out of things to say, so I made my excuses. Around halfway through the evening, our team hadn’t won anything, and the mood of the table had turned slightly sour. It was at this point that the young woman came over to chat again. Through a haze of wine, I remember feeling irritated.

Finally the ceremony ended, and we shuffled out to the cloakroom, where she and I encountered each other for the third time. Again, a sense of overfamiliarity lingered as we said our goodbyes. As my colleagues and I were heading to the door, one of them asked me who she was. I went into a diatribe about how that woman was such a phoney, pretending that we knew each other well. I overegged it entirely for the benefit of my audience. “I can’t stand her,” I finished dramatically.

“I’m standing right behind you,” a voice said. I turned around, and there she was. When such a moment occurs, adrenaline floods your body alongside a cold dread, and then you just have to sit in the murk of what you have created. I opened my mouth to apologise but nothing came out.

Although this is someone whose name I don’t remember, and who I am unlikely to recognise if I saw them again, I think about this moment with surprising regularity. I think about what it must have been like to hear someone talk about you like that, but I also wonder what possessed me to say all of those things that weren’t even real, or true.

I wish I could tell her I’m sorry, and that I was probably saying all of those things about myself, and it was definitely not about her at all. That, actually, I was in a really unhappy place in my life, and while alcohol should never be an excuse, it made me a nastier version of myself. I wonder how many of these apologies I owe to people.

Poorna Bell is a journalist and author. Her latest book, She Wanted More, is out now.

Annie Lord: ‘I gave it about a day, then I dumped him. I thought I was rotten, so if someone liked me there must be something wrong with them’

We were in year 8. I don’t remember much about him. Only that he was covered in freckles and was very bony, all elbows and knees. To me he appeared quite conventionally attractive with his well-proportioned face, but he was in the nerdy group so that wouldn’t have counted for anything. He came back from a holiday with malaria, which I thought was pretty exciting back then.

Around him, everything else seemed to fade into nothing. My throat would go dry when we spoke, and it was hard to get my words out. I realised after a while that this must be what fancying someone felt like. Eventually, he fancied me, too, and asked me to be his girlfriend. Well, he asked someone to ask me, as was customary back then.

It wasn’t long after I said yes that something started to shift. What was once light and uncertain was now concrete: he was my boyfriend. Now there were rules we had to follow. People would expect us to kiss, hold hands, be together all the time. The intensity that I had once enjoyed now felt suffocating.

When people found out, there wasn’t much of a commotion because I wasn’t a very notable character. I was Vicky’s best friend, the blond girl who went bright red when anyone spoke to her. But I remember sitting on the field during PE and one of the popular girls saying to me, “Oh, how sweet, Pete’s finally got a girlfriend.” It was immediately horrifying. Her comment seemed to confirm all my deepest fears. There must be something wrong with him – that’s why no one else wanted him.

I gave it about a day and then I dumped him. He would have seen Vicky coming across the field and known what was coming. He took it well. He wasn’t horrible to me, like some men I’ve rejected. I felt an instant dizzying relief, but then alongside it, digging its nails in, this fear that maybe I’d made a mistake.

I’d go on to repeat this pattern over the course of my life with lots of different men. Liking them and then having a feeling of terror when they started to like me. I would watch them move on to other women, look at their photos together on Instagram and think, why were you so scared of that being you?

It’s only in the last year, through therapy, that I have fully unpacked what was going on. I was going through puberty, my body was changing, and a deep feeling of wrongness sunk down into my very tissue. I thought I was rotten, so if someone liked me there must be something wrong with them. That girl’s comment during PE confirmed this.

We can be so imaginative when it comes to love. But when it comes to rejection we can’t imagine all the million reasons a person might not want to be with you: there’s just you and why you’re not good enough. I hope he knows it was nothing to do with him. I hope it didn’t make him scared of intimacy, or trap him in a pattern.

When I see kids in love, I think about how lucky they are. It must be so incredible to love that young, to feel it that much, to enter into intimacy slowly and safely with someone you trust. We could have had that, but I ran from it. I ruined it for both of us. I’m really sorry for him because I robbed us of that experience, but I’m also really sorry for myself.

Annie Lord is a writer and author. Her latest book, The Project, is out now.

Nikesh Shukla: ‘I grew up in fear of being told off, not really understanding what I did wrong in the first place. And I don’t want you to feel like that’

Dear kids

I don’t know what came over me. I’m sorry. That’s all I can say. I know it’s not nice to be shouted at. And, look, I think you and your sister could take a little responsibility for waiting until I’m concentrating to start bickering. Why did you wait until I sat down at my desk to work on my novel before getting into a fight about the big green Lego tile? Seriously? We have two of them! I know one of them is supersize, but stick them together and you get a mega-tile! Imagine the house you could build on a mega-tile! Just stop bickering!

I think I have let this apology run away from me somewhat. It’s almost as pompous as what I said to you at the time. When I relayed this story to a friend later on, she howled with laughter and called me a pretentious [redacted swear word]. I believe I said – well, shouted, at the top of my voice: “I don’t have a regular job. I am in that room creating universes and moving characters around them. And when you pull me out of that universe and back into this boring home because you can’t remember who used the green Lego tile last, that universe dies. Just a little. But it dies.”

Oh God, typing that out you can really hear how ridiculous it sounds. How high-minded. You’d really have to think what you do is special in order to shout that. What you don’t know is, at the time, I was writing a scene in a comic book about a man tripping over a discarded apple while running for the bus. Put that in your imagined universe and smoke it.

I used to think a lot about what sort of parent I would be. Of course, you only ever really have your parents as the first example. My own mum and dad made me feel as if they were never in the wrong. If they told me and your aunt off, they didn’t ever really explain themselves. I grew up in fear of being told off, not understanding what I did wrong in the first place. And I don’t want you to feel like that. Because there have definitely been times when I’ve been cross with you because I was tired, or stressed by work, or interrupted having a gossipy text exchange with a friend and thought, hold on a minute, I’m the blinkin’ adult here! I must regain control.

None of those situations are because you actually did anything that bad. They were all me. And so I have tried my best to apologise when I realise that the telling off that upset you was because of something else. I didn’t apologise to you that day, about being Mr Universe-Creator. As soon as I sat back down at my desk, I realised how ridiculous I had been. And you were both quiet again, playing away, creating your own universes. When I checked back in on you later, I saw that you had ended up working together, using all the green tiles to build a mega-structure. Which I suppose was a good thing, but I hated myself for making you do it because of my anger.

That comic book is out now. And it’s about a dad who can’t really control his anger. And, it turns out, the call was coming from inside the house the entire time. I am so sorry I shouted something incredibly pompous at you, and, to be honest, apology aside, there is no way of telling this story without looking like a complete pilchard.

Love, Dad

Nikesh Shukla is an author and screenwriter.

title: Budget 2027: A Political battle to frame what comes next
summary: With Budget 2027 just over a week away, the political battle is already being fought over how announcements will be framed. From energy and housing to tax and welfare, Fiachra Ó Cionnaith looks at how the Government and Opposition are preparing competing narratives about what the public can expect.
full_text:
Budgets might be all about the numbers, but how they add up for the public always comes down to framing.

And with Budget 2027 just over a week away, that reality is now to the forefront of political minds, with parties increasingly pushing forward their own narratives to explain what Tuesday 6 October's announcements will mean for those who matter most.

For Government, the message is that this Budget is focused on securing Ireland's financial safety in a time of geo-political uncertainty, while trying to make life a little easier for hard working individuals in the process.

For the Opposition, many of the already leaked plans are further proof that - in their eyes at least - those in power remain out of touch with the stark financial realities facing struggling households across the country.

And, while they are all smiles in public, the recent skirmishes over housing policy proposals are another sign that Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael are keen to prioritise their own best interests as much as the Government's itself, just in case events one day overtake Coalition collegiality.

Lots is at stake as the competing elements of Irish politics prepare their frames for the full Budget 2027 picture to come.

Key battlegrounds

While the Budget is still more than a week away, it is already clear that the most prominent political framing battles are likely to be fought on three key areas - the energy crisis, housing, and the split between tax cuts and social welfare supports.

The reason for the first of those issues is obvious, with the energy crisis and April's highly contentious fuel protests continuing to be one of the most dominant factors in politics throughout this year, a situation the ongoing US-Iran stand-off shows is unlikely to change anytime soon.

Petrol and diesel prices above €2 a litre, household electricity bill price rises in the region of 9% during Budget week, and the continuing debate over whether energy credits or alternative temporary measures like fuel allowance increases are best mean the situation will be central to how Budget 2027 is seen.

So too will be the latest attempt to address the housing crisis, with the pre-Budget debates over rent credit supports, an increase on the help to buy scheme ceiling and first time buyers stamp duty all coming at the same time that property prices far exceed the Celtic Tiger era with a record 17,885 people needing emergency accommodation last month alone.

As ever when it comes to the Budget, tax and State supports are also at the core of discussions, with potential plans to increase the entry point for the highest rate of tax to €46,000, loosen existing inheritance tax limits, and create a new investment scheme competing for funding with the traditional State pension and welfare priorities.

Government focus

Much of the Government's framing of these three areas has been on how it is doing all it can in uncertain international times, a point pushed home by Tánaiste and Fine Gael leader Simon Harris in the Dail on Thursday.

Speaking during a leaders questions debate on the energy crisis, Mr Harris - who is facing into his first Budget as Minister for Finance - responded to Sinn Féin's Pearse Doherty by saying while an energy and fuel crisis exists, the Coalition can only do so much, arguing:

"It's [the crisis] not by any decision taken in Dáil Eireann, it's because the Strait of Hormuz is closed. It's because there's been the bombing of Iran. You or I didn't take a decision, let's not blow up the egos of people in this House."

That point is one which, the Coalition argues, has some merit, with Government TDs arguing in recent days that any measures taken to help address the situation should be seen in this context.

The latest fuel excise duty cuts extension from November until February or March, as confirmed by Fianna Fáil TD and Minister for Public Expenditure Jack Chambers on RTE Radio this week, is about giving businesses, commuters and hauliers breathing space in difficult economic times rather than avoiding making a tough decision, the argument goes.

The likely €5 increase in the fuel allowance and its potential extension into Spring next year will also, Coalition members insist, support households most in need while not over-straining the Exchequer with expensive once-off measures.

And, while this could mean the increase to the weekly State pension may be €7.50 rather than last year's €10 as money needs to be spread carefully to protect Ireland from the global energy crisis uncertainty, those in solid jobs will benefit from a likely raising of the highest rate of income tax threshold to €46,000 as part of what the Tánaiste has described as "a workers' budget".

According to this Coalition Budget frame these are sensible points for potentially difficult times ahead, added to by the attempt in recent weeks by Minister Chambers in particular to downplay - for now anyway - the height of the financial bounce people should expect from the 6 October Budget.

Government is doing all it can to balance the books and keep the country safe from the choppy waters elsewhere, but all going well the public can still expect "modest" gains and a "few hundred euro" extra in total this year as well as a cost of living package to help those most in need, is the message.

Sensible pragmatism during straightened times, sure what's wrong with that? Well, quite a bit, believe the Opposition.

Opposition focus

Unlike the Government's Budget frame pointing to what will be announced, the Opposition's narrative is instead focused on what will not be, a contradiction again underlined at leaders' questions this week.

Speaking in the Dáil, Sinn Féin's finance spokesperson Pearse Doherty mirrored comments from party leader Mary Lou McDonald earlier in the week by warning the Government it does "not understand the pressure that people are under".

While acknowledging the unavoidable consequences of the Strait of Hormuz stand-off, a situation even the modest sturdy of opposition TDs would struggle to blame on the Coalition, Deputy Doherty said the upcoming budget risks leaving vulnerable people at further risk.

On three occasions he called for a €400 energy credit to be introduced, a position it is by now widely acknowledged Government is unlikely to agree to introducing.

Sinn Féin has also recently called for the universal social charge to be scrapped for the first €40,000 of a worker's salary, for a €10 per day cap on childcare costs, and for a windfall tax on energy companies - all of which focus on what the Coalition is not doing rather than what it is.

That approach has been mirrored in recent weeks by the Social Democrats too, with the party's recent pre-Dáil think-in hearing calls for a €400 energy credit for households earning under €70,000, increasing core social welfare rates to €15, while the Labour Party wants to see a similar energy credit, a €16 social welfare rate and the second tier of child benefit, among other matters.

Speaking in the Dáil this week, Labour's public expenditure spokesperson Ged Nash also noted that the Government's climate action plan for this year has yet to be published, a situation also highlighted by Green Party leader Roderic O Gorman alongside his demands for the public transport ticket price rise to be reversed at his party's own recent pre-Dáil think in.

When alternative budgets are published this coming week, expect further differences with Government to be added to with calls for improved help to buy supports, an increase in the rent tax credit and other housing aides - a weak point for the Coalition that the Opposition will be keen to keep in the spotlight.

A dis-united Coalition?

While much of the pre-Budget political rows are between the Government and Opposition, it should be noted of course that this year's budget build-up has also seen some division between Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael, particularly on the housing question.

That situation was most apparent in the aftermath of calls by Fianna Fáil TD Seamus McGrath for the 1% stamp duty for first time buyers to be scrapped.

A sensible measure that will help people buy a home, Deputy McGrath argued.

Not so for the Tánaiste, who told reporters earlier this month that "there are no proposals in relation to the Programme for Government around stamp duty, and therefore at this moment in time, I'm not proposing bringing forward such measures."

The Fine Gael leader has separately noted that such a move did not work as well as hoped, to put it mildly, in the final years of the Celtic Tiger boom.

Mr Harris has, it should be acknowledged, also said that "this is not about one party in Government or another party in Government", and perhaps he is right.

However, the remark is known to have irked some on Fianna Fáil's backbenches, not helped by separate ongoing internal debate between the Coalition parties over Minister for Housing James Browne's proposal to increase the help to buy scheme limit by €20,000.

Asked about the apparent pre-Budget differences by reporters in New York, Taoiseach Micheál Martin somewhat aptly put his best diplomatic foot forward.

Disagreements, he responded, what disagreements?

"We haven't raised help to buy, and I haven't raised that at any of the meetings at leadership level.

"That's not the case as you've asserted. I've just said, all of the issues you've been reading about have been discussed by all of the leaders, so don't believe everything that you see."

Money talks

Regardless of the competing political frames and narratives being pushed on the public by parties, ultimately the real impact of Budget 2027 will be felt in the pockets and bank accounts of ordinary households across Ireland.

So, in just over a week's time, will the overriding message be the Tánaiste's "help is coming", or Pearse Doherty's "you don't understand the pressure people are under"?

And, if things go wrong over the next 12 months, will it be 'blame Donald Trump and Iran', or blame people just a little closer to home?

Despite the political arguments taking place, money - and whether you have more or less of it come Tuesday 6 October - is what will really talk.

It is a reality all the politicians can see, regardless of the frame they choose to look through.

title: ‘Congress part of every conspiracy’: CM Yogi amid 'dissent within EC' row
full_text:
Yogi Adityanath hits out at opposition over SIR row

NEW DELHI: Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath defended the Election Commission amid the "dissent within the poll body" row, while slamming the Congress party for "creating confusion and targeting constitutional institutions". Tearing into the rival Congress for criticisng the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, the Uttar Pradesh CM said: "The current SIR exercise was not the first such revision undertaken by the Election Commission, pointing to similar exercises conducted in 1952, 1957, 1961, 1965–66 and 2003." "Regarding the SIR (Special Intensive Revision), the confusion that has been consistently created by them (opposition parties), it is not as if the current Election Commission is the first to undertake such an exercise; in the past—often under Congress-led governments—similar exercises were conducted in 1952, 1957, 1961, 1965–66, and even in 2003. Despite this history, the uproar raised by the Congress, Samajwadi Party, RJD, and other parties over the current SIR exercise is extremely unfortunate. " He said the Election Commission had already clarified that eligible voters who were left out would be given an opportunity to submit the required form. He also referred to the Supreme Court’s position on the Election Commission’s action regarding Form 6. "All three Election Commissioners came before the press and clarified the situation. Regarding SIR, directions had already been issued that all eligible voters who were left out would be given an opportunity to fill the form. The Supreme Court has also upheld the Election Commission's action regarding Form 6. Despite this, putting the Election Commission and Chief Election Commissioners in the dock, questioning every constitutional institution and attempting to tarnish India's image globally is extremely unfortunate. Congress and its allies should control their irresponsible actions. There should be no place for violence, vandalism or misinformation in a democracy." Adityanath further accused the Congress and other opposition parties of undermining constitutional institutions and democratic values for political interests. "The approach of the Congress and opposition parties has always been to be a part of every conspiracy to harm the constitutional institutions of India and weaken the democratic values ​​for their political interests, due to which the world's largest democracy can be harmed. It is surprising that the current actions and rhetoric of the country's main opposition party and other parties associated with the UPA alliance are extremely irresponsible and damaging to democratic values. " Adityanath also criticised the Congress over its objections to EVMs, noting that Congress governments had been formed at the Centre and in several states through elections conducted using the machines. He linked the criticism to what he described as a broader pattern of questioning democratic institutions. "The EVMs, through which Congress governments have also been formed at the Centre and in several states, have been called a black box, raising questions about India's electoral system and the country's democratic values. Recall that on June 25, 1975, Congress sinned by undermining the Constitution by imposing the Emergency. Congress-led governments also repeatedly dismissed elected governments of opposition parties through unconstitutional means. Their actions have repeatedly compromised the country's internal and external security. Questioning the valour of the Indian armed forces during the Balakot airstrike and attempting to cast doubt on the bravery of Indian soldiers during Operation Sindoor are examples of this approach."

Join conversation

Share your thoughts in the comments

Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

The remarks come amid a major political confrontation over reported objections raised by two Election Commissioners to decisions related to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. Opposition parties have demanded action against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, an immediate halt to the SIR exercise and fresh elections in states where polls have already been held. The ruling BJP, however, defended the Election Commission, saying differences expressed by Election Commissioners during internal deliberations demonstrated that the poll panel was functioning democratically rather than under a “dictatorial” system

End of Article

title: Nandigram and Rejinagar bypoll: Ballot without the battle
summary: Bypolls for two Assembly constituencies in West Bengal Nandigram and Rejinagar scheduled for October 6, are turning out to be an electoral exercise without much contest on the ground. Shrabana Chatterjee and Senjuti Sengupta report on the dropouts and intimidation that candidates from non-BJP parties are allegedly facing
full_text:
In West Bengal, the Bharatiya Janata Party has the support of 207 MLAs in the 294-member Assembly. Two constituencies are up for bypolls, a situation created because the elected representatives won from other constituencies in the State elections earlier this year.

Editorial | Freezing democracy: On the Election Commission of India and West Bengal

The main parties in the fray are the BJP, the Trinamool Congress, the Congress, and the Left. This is the first election in which former Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee’s Trinamool will fight on the symbol of a footballer rather than its flowers-and-grass insignia.

Nandigram: a fight for prestige

The Nandigram Assembly seat, with 17 panchayats, has about 2.5 lakh people, of whom about 27% of the electorate is Muslim. This is Suvendu Adhikari’s home district.

Mr. Adhikari has stated several times that the constituency is a prestige fight for him.

Also Read: YouTuber behind Kolkata restaurant beef row, influencers, RJ and actors funded by BJP during Bengal polls

The constituency

During the Vietnam War that peaked in the 1960s, West Bengal’s Left Front, powerful in the State then, protested on behalf of the country, with the slogan: “Amar naam, tomar naam, Vietnam, Vietnam [My name, your name, Vietnam, Vietnam].” In 2007, during the movement against forcible land acquisition for a chemical hub, which saw 14 people die, the Left Front government was still in power.

But this time, the same slogan went against it: it became “Amar naam, tomar naam, Nandigram, Nandigram [My name your name, Nandigram, Nandigram].”

Nandigram, a predominantly rural Assembly constituency in coastal Purba Medinipur district of West Bengal, has been synonymous with political change. The fight against forcible land acquisition brought the downfall of the Left Front government in 2011.

In 2021, when Mr. Adhikari defeated former Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee by a margin of 1,956 votes in Nandigram, the constituency brought to the fore a new leader.

In 2026, he contested and won the seat by a margin of about 9,665 votes. Since he was elected from two constituencies, Nandigram and Bhabanipur, he decided to represent Bhabanipur, where he defeated Ms. Banerjee again.

Key candidates

The BJP has fielded Hasirani Rath, the mother of Mr. Adhikari’s slain personal assistant.

Ms. Hasirani has an emotional appeal because she lost her son in the post-poll violence in West Bengal this year. Her son, Chandranath Rath, was shot dead at point-blank range on May 6, just two days after the BJP came to power in the State for the first time, ending the 15-year-old Mamata Banerjee rule.

“This place has been nurtured by Suvendu Adhikari. Of course he is the only one who will win here,” Ms. Hashirani says, after she offered puja at 13 local temples in the constituency as part of her poll campaign in the last week of September.

“Most people in Nandigram have spontaneously accepted me as the daughter of Nandigram and the mother of their homes,” Ms. Hasirani says.

She insists that Adhikari will remain the leader of the people of Nandigram, and it is not victory that she is concerned about. “We want the margin of the victory to be 1.5 lakh votes,” she adds.

The Chief Minister had urged the people of Nandigram to ensure the highest-ever margin of victory in the constituency.

Former CM Banerjee initially announced her support for Sanchita Pradhan Dey, who withdrew from the contest. Then she supported the Congress nominee from Nandigram, Milan Pradhan. Within hours, he was arrested in a 19-year-old case. He was a leader and activist who was part of Nandigram’s land movement in 2007. Mr. Pradhan has been sent to judicial custody till October 3. His bail plea at the Calcutta High Court was denied on September 22.

“He has always been here at public events; why was he not arrested before? Why arrest him now when he became the Congress candidate?” Arpita, his wife, said in a video message shared by State Congress leaders.

The Left Front has fielded Communist Party of India’s Shanti Gopal Giri for the bypoll.

Key issues and campaign

In the Nandigram bypoll, the Congress is running its campaign on its candidate being arrested by the West Bengal police. “We are all Milan Pradhan. He cannot be here because he was wrongfully arrested. We are all standing here as the candidate,” a campaign member of the Congress said while asking people to vote in the party’s favour.

“Even Mamata didi has asked everyone to support our candidate,” the Congress workers tell people of Nandigram as they go from house to house. The arrest of Pradhan has brought the Congress leadership in West Bengal together and evoked a strong response from the party’s high command. Leader of Opposition in Parliament, Rahul Gandhi, called it “political revenge, the murder of democracy”.

“The BJP has no faith in fair elections — that’s why it wants to cling to power, sometimes through vote theft, sometimes through stealing governments, and sometimes through stealing parties,” Mr. Gandhi said on X.

Meanwhile, the BJP is driving its by-poll campaign on the emotional appeal of a mother who has lost her child. Mr. Adhikari accompanied Hasirani when she filed her nomination papers.

Addressing a gathering after the nomination, the Chief Minister exuded confidence by saying that the BJP will win by “such a big margin in Nandigram that no one has ever imagined”. He said that Chandranath Rath’s biggest sin was that he was his aide.

He promised to fulfil all the promises made to the people of Nandigram.

What the electorate says

Purnima, 50, from Gopalchak area in Nandigram is emotional about the mother’s loss. “A mother lost her child in these politics. We are bound to vote for her,” she says.

Amina Bibi, 65, from the Mohammadpur area says that people of Nandigram have always spoken truth to power and she does not shy away from speaking the truth now.

“I fought shoulder to shoulder with Suvendu during the Nandigram protests. But since he became CM, he has not dared to come back here because he knows he has not done anything for us,” she says. A man in his mid-50 from Mohammadpur in Nandigram who did not want to be named, says, “This is not a democracy where there is no fair election and people are not allowed to participate. In a democracy every candidate should get a fair chance to campaign and contest. That is missing here.”

Rejinagar: wall graffiti speaks

Rejinagar constituency has over 2.56 Lakh voters and about 69% of the electorate in the constituency are Muslim voters. The Bhagirathi river, a distributary of Ganga passes through the constituency, which spans over two blocks: Beldanga I and II, comprising nearly 14 panchayats. A predominately rural constituency, the region has little employment opportunities and youth migrate for work.

The constituency

Rejinagar is located less than 15 kilometres from Plassey, where a war between the East India Company and Nawab Siraj-u-Daullah of Murshidabad almost 270 years changed the history of the subcontinent forever.

The constituency, located in West Bengal’s Murshidabad district, was a highlight of the 2026 Assembly polls. Aam Janata Unnyan Party (AJUP) leader Humayun Kabir’s had attempted to construct a mosque styled on the lines of the Babri masjid in Ayodhya.

Mr. Kabir’s campaign in the 2026 Assembly polls on the issue of construction of the mosque, split the Muslim votes, polarised Hindus, and eventually was one of the reasons that led to fall of the 15-year-old Trinamool Congress government. Kabir, who was expelled from the Trinamool Congress, set up AJUP and won elections from Naoda and Rejinagar in the district. He vacated Rejinagar where his margin of victory was over 58,000 votes.

The project of construction of the Babri-style mosque next to a national highway has been stalled and the site that had hundreds of people thronging before the Assembly polls, is desolate.

The constituency had witnessed violent protests during the anti-CAA [Citizenship Amendment Act] protests in 2019. In 2024 there was an explosion during a Ram Navami procession, which left about 20 people injured.

Key candidates

The by-polls at Rejinagar have been necessitated after Humayun Kabir resigned from his Rejinagar seat on June 4. The AJUP chairperson has fielded his son Golam Nabi Azad. Neither is campaigning in a big way, saying there is intimidation by the administration, controlled by the ruling party.

The Banerjee-backed faction of the Trinamool Congress has fielded Rabiul Alam Chowdhury, a former MLA, as their candidate. Chowdhury had represented the seat for three terms, first being elected from the Congress in 2011, and later as a Trinamool Congress nominee. Chowdhury too had said he would withdraw from the contest, but later decided to reconsider, after intervention from Banerjee.

Congress fielded Abdullahil Kafi, Leader of the Opposition from the Murshidabad Zila Parishad. The Ritabrata Banerjee-led TMC faction (Democratic TMC) fielded Safiuzzaman S.K.

CPI (M) has fielded Saeed Asad Ali. The BJP is hoping for a split of minority votes and that a polarisation of Hindu votes will make way for its victory, the BJP is banking on a polarisation of Hindu votes and have fielded Sakharav Sarkar.

Key issues and campaign

The leaders of the AJUP and Banerjee-backed Trinamool Congress have alleged intimidation by the police and said that they are not being allowed to contest. Mr. Kabir has decided to stay away from the campaigning, accusing the local police of slapping fake cases against his workers and arresting them.

According to Mr. Kabir, “Fifteen of my workers have been arrested by the police, while many have fled to other places fearing the police’s constant threats. This is terrifying. Police are picking up everyone they see with me. They have become the BJP’s agents. I can’t risk my workers’ lives,” he says. The MLA was also called for questioning to Berhampore Police Station on September 21 and 23, in relation to a viral audio clip that pointed to subject matter pertaining to communal tension.

Mr. Kabir adds that his son is still visiting some areas, “But we stopped major campaigning. I will communicate with people and campaign for my son through Facebook only,” he says.

On September 19, West Bengal police arrested Saiful Islam, an independent candidate from Rejinagar, who has close associations with the AJUP leadership. While the graffiti of the Opposition candidates has come up all across the constituency, the only candidate who is actively campaigning is the BJP’s Sarkar.

While the party offices of the candidates in Opposition wear a desolate look, the party office of the BJP at Rejinagar is bustling with activity. “TMC has not done anything for this area in the last 15 years. Humayun Kabir’s corruption has also been exposed. He duped people of crores in the name of his Babri Masjid replica project. The public is not foolish. They want a change,” Sarkar says. The BJP candidate says that he is fighting this election on a development pitch and getting good response from people across communities.

While Mr. Sakharav is campaigning across the constituency, the graffiti of Opposition candidates — the hammer and sickle of CPI(M), hand of Congress, football player of Ms. Banerjee’s All India Trinamool Congress, and whistle of AJUP — are on the walls of Rejinagar.

What the electorate says

Mohsin Sheikh, who resides near Beldanga Police Station in Rejinagar, says, “The election looks very different this time. There is not much show of parties and their candidates, unlike previous elections. A strange silence has captured the area.”

There are voters who lament the lack of development in the region, health facilities, and transport. “The nearest hospital in our area is 5-6 km away. Those who stay in the part of the constituency which is connected to the national highway may still get proper transport to reach there in emergency cases. But what about the people from the other side of the river?” says Nafisa Bibi, who runs a teashop at Saktipur village, which is around 12 km from the ferry-ghat.

Hamid, a street vendor, stops at the boundary of the under-construction mosque. “It was a good initiative. When it’s completed, everybody will come to pray here from even the neighbouring districts. Our business will grow,” he says, as he prepares his jhaalmuri mix.
